The IKeyMaster
In previous chapters, you've seen C# interfaces used to treat several different classes as if
they were the same type of thing. Here, we will use IKeyMaster in a slightly different way.
As mentioned previously, the only things that a /ocNedDoor needs to know about Dray
are Dray's facing and keyCount (i.e., the number of keys Dray has). So, in this case, we'll
use the I.eyMaster interface for encapsulation, which is the idea of isolating your classes
from each other so that they can only see or modify information that they really need
access to. Dray has many public fields and methods, but if /ocNedDoor thinks that it
is dealing with an instance of I.eyMaster (rather than an instance of Dray), it can only
access the public methods and properties in the I.eyMaster interface. This protects all
the other public fields and methods of Dray from being accessed by /ocNedDoor.

Introduced for the first time in The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past, the Hookshot is
one of the most iconic items in the Zelda series. Now, you can see how this item might
have worked if it were part of the first Zelda game. In Dungeon Delver, the Grappler is a

the wall, including pulling them over previously impassable red tiles. The Grappler also
has two secondary abilities: It can cause a small amount of damage to enemies, and it
can pull PickUps to Dray.
To be honest with you, the Grappler implementation was one of the most difficult
revisions for this third edition of the book. In the second edition, the Grappler was
implemented as a bit of a hack that included code that took over Dray's movement by
setting the enabled field to false on the Dray script. As mentioned in the tip earlier in

SHORTING OPERATORS AND FUNCTION CALLS
The line at // i in Code Listing 36.26 demonstrates an important use of the short-
ing OR operator:
if ( Pode  eMode.gadget __ currentGadget.Gadget&ancel() ) ^ // i
If code execution reaches this line, and Dray is in eMode.gadget mode, Gadget
&ancel() is called on the currentGadget (attempting to cancel the gadget use),
and if that is successful, the callback to GadgetIsDone() will set Pode to eMode.
idle. This call to Gadget&ancel() is primarily used to turn the gadget off (e.g., if
Dray is hit when the Grappler is doing anything other than pulling Dray to it, this
will cause the Grappler go back to its idle state), but it also allows an IGadget to
prevent knockback on Dray by returning false (though Dray will still take damage).
If, on the other hand, Dray is not in eMode.gadget mode, Gadget&ancel() is not
called. This is because of the shorting nature of the __ operator. If the first condi-
tion (the Pode  eMode.gadget before the __ ) is true, then the __ operator
shorts, and the second condition ( currentGadget.Gadget&ancel() ) is never
evaluated. Thus, currentGadget.Gadget&ancel() is only ever called if Dray is in
eMode.gadget mode.
Now, Dray has the ability to use an IGadget, but we still need to make a gadget for
them to use.
Building the Grappler
Now, we'll make the Grappler itself. This will take the form of a GameObject child of

in the middle of the room or the north wall. Either one will end the grapple with
Dray on an unsafe lava tile, which should reset Dray's position to the doorway
and deduct 2 points of health (which is one full circle of health).
Now that you've implemented the Grappler and tested it, there's only one more thing
left to do before this level is ready to play.

If you do continue with this project, here are some additional things you can add to
make it a more interesting game:
1. Implement the Spiker enemy. The prefab is already there, but it needs a little work.
Instructions for implementing it are in a long comment at the top of the Spiker C#

new behaviors.

sword that shoots out when Link is at full health. There is a second sword in the
Swords image file that could be used for this.
